extraction.body: Another safety researcher has walked away from OpenAI, with David Robinson becoming the latest employee to resign while raising alarms about the company's internal culture. Robinson's departure adds to growing concerns about how the ChatGPT maker handles AI safety as it races toward artificial general intelligence, marking yet another high-profile exit from the company's safety team. David Robinson didn't mince words when he walked away from OpenAI. The safety researcher's resignation letter, obtained by TechCrunch, paints a picture of a company whose internal culture has fundamentally shifted as it chases the artificial general intelligence prize. Robinson acknowledges he's become "something of a cliché" - another AI safety employee issuing dire warnings while heading for the exit. But that self-awareness doesn't diminish the weight of his concerns about how OpenAI operates behind closed doors. Robinson's departure follows a string of high-profile exits from OpenAI's safety teams, including co-founder Ilya Sutskever and safety researcher Jan Leike earlier this year. Both left citing concerns that the company was prioritizing flashy product releases over the careful safety work needed for increasingly powerful AI systems. OpenAI has been sprinting toward what CEO Sam Altman calls "superintelligence" - AI systems that could surpass human capabilities across virtually all domains. That race has intensified pressure inside the company, with multiple former employees describing a culture that's shifted from cautious research to aggressive commercialization. Safety researchers join OpenAI drawn by the mission of developing beneficial AI, then leave frustrated by what they see as corner-cutting and cultural problems that make their work impossible. Robinson's resignation adds another data point to this troubling trend. What makes Robinson's departure particularly significant is his willingness to go public with specific cultural criticisms. Previous exits have been more diplomatically handled, with departing researchers offering vague concerns about "alignment" between personal values and company direction. Robinson appears to be taking a more direct approach. The safety team brain drain comes as OpenAI faces mounting external pressure over its development practices. Competitors like Anthropic have positioned themselves as the more safety-conscious alternative, while regulators worldwide are scrambling to understand and oversee AI development. Industry observers note that losing safety talent isn't just a PR problem for OpenAI - it's a technical one. These researchers possess deep knowledge of the company's systems and the specific risks they pose. OpenAI transformed from a research lab into a commercial powerhouse worth over $80 billion, but that metamorphosis has apparently cost the company some of its founding principles. For Robinson, the cultural shift became impossible to ignore. His decision to speak publicly about a "broken" culture suggests the problems run deeper than typical workplace friction - pointing instead to fundamental disagreements about how AI development should proceed. The question now is whether OpenAI will address the underlying issues driving these departures or continue losing the safety expertise it claims to value. With each resignation, the company's credibility on AI safety takes another hit, potentially undermining its position as regulators and competitors circle. Robinson's resignation crystallizes a growing crisis of confidence in OpenAI's commitment to safe AI development. As the company races toward superintelligence, losing the very researchers tasked with ensuring that journey doesn't end in catastrophe sends a troubling signal to investors, regulators, and the public. The real test will be whether OpenAI can rebuild trust with its safety teams before more critical expertise walks out the door.

extraction.body: By his own admission, David Robinson is “something of a cliché”: an employee at a leading AI company who issues a dire warning while resigning from their job. In an essay published in The Atlantic , Robinson said he led the writing of safety reports that accompanied OpenAI’s major product launches. He also said that with three-and-a-half years at OpenAI, he is “among the longest-tenured employees at the company.” Now he’s quitting, because in his view, the company’s “culture is broken.” In some ways, Robinson’s comments echo those of Jacob Coxon, who worked as a researcher at both OpenAI and Anthropic before quitting and declaring that these companies are “gambling with our lives.” Coxon’s comments led to a broader debate about AI safety, with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei unveiling a plan for more cautious AI development ; AI executives met with President Donald Trump this week and signed what appeared to be hastily written, non-binding pledge to implement more safety controls . But in Robinson’s view, the debate needs to go beyond “specific rules or new laws,” addressing the overall culture at these companies. And while much of the reporting around OpenAI has focused on how the company’s CEO Sam Altman lost the trust of former colleagues , Robinson’s essay suggests that OpenAI’s culture issues are the same as those of Silicon Valley at large. “OpenAI has thrived by trial and error (which it calls ‘iterative deployment’), looking for problems and improving its guardrails in response,” he wrote. “But this approach, by its very nature, guarantees periodic failures — and the scale of those failures is growing as systems get more capable.” Pointing to the recent breach of Hugging Face systems by OpenAI agents, as well as continuing revelations of OpenAI discovering more rogue agents , Robinson argued, “An environment where things like this can happen is no place to grow artificial minds that could be smarter than we are and that might not do what we want them to.” Given the increased risk, Robinson argued that frontier AI companies need to start operating “like nuclear-power plants or busy airports, with layers of redundancy and careful, time-consuming planning, so that the occasional and inevitable human error does not open a door to disaster.” But Robinson said that in his time at OpenAI, he “never encountered a colleague who had experience making airplanes fly safely or nuclear reactors run without melting down, or helping the financial system grow without collapsing.” In response to Robinson’s essay, OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company continues to improve its safety measures. “We’re making sure our models don’t become more capable than we can safely manage and secure, and we pause training or hold back models when we need to slow down,” Pusateri said in a statement. “We’re making significant changes to strengthen security in our research and testing environments, train models to not just complete tasks but do so responsibly, expand our work with third-party evaluators, and improve real-time monitoring so we can detect and respond to concerning behavior earlier in the training process .” Beyond calling for changes in OpenAI’s culture, Robinson also said it’s time to ask bigger questions about alignment — something that he admitted could sound “touchy-feely,” but he said it’s critical as companies’ current “measures of how well” AI systems “match human values are coarse.” “The smarter the industry lets models grow while these problems remain unsolved, the more dangerous our situation becomes,” he said. Robinson’s departure was first reported by Business Insider . In his essay, he also acknowledged that he’s following an apparently a common step in the AI whistleblower playbook: He’s hired a PR firm . But he insisted, “The decision to speak out is mine alone.” “Perhaps I should have stayed and fought for fundamental shifts in our staffing and culture, but in practice, my colleagues and I were so busy sprinting that we seldom had the chance to consider big changes, much less to actually make them,” Robinson said. “That’s why I concluded that stronger incentives for safety — coming from outside the company — are a big part of getting this right.” World’s first enhanced geothermal power plant completed in just 23 months Tim De Chant Google releases Gemini 4 Argon, called its most powerful model yet Lucas Ropek The Pentagon taps Elon Musk and Palmer Luckey to help decide what the military should do next Dominic-Madori Davis OpenAI launches Dots, its bubbly agentic avatar Lucas Ropek AMD will acquire Fei-Fei Li’s World Labs for $8.2B Tim Fernholz Viral AI agent Instinct raises $1B Series C at a $10B valuation Sarah Perez

In an essay published in The Atlantic , Robinson said he led the writing of safety reports that accompanied OpenAI’s major product launches. He also said that with three-and-a-half years at OpenAI, he is “among the longest-tenured employees at the company.” Now he’s quitting, because in his view, the company’s “culture is broken.”

In some ways, Robinson’s comments echo those of Jacob Coxon, who worked as a researcher at both OpenAI and Anthropic before quitting and declaring that these companies are “gambling with our lives.” Coxon’s comments led to a broader debate about AI safety, with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei unveiling a plan for more cautious AI development ; AI executives met with President Donald Trump this week and signed what appeared to be hastily written, non-binding pledge to implement more safety controls .

But in Robinson’s view, the debate needs to go beyond “specific rules or new laws,” addressing the overall culture at these companies. And while much of the reporting around OpenAI has focused on how the company’s CEO Sam Altman lost the trust of former colleagues , Robinson’s essay suggests that OpenAI’s culture issues are the same as those of Silicon Valley at large.

“OpenAI has thrived by trial and error (which it calls ‘iterative deployment’), looking for problems and improving its guardrails in response,” he wrote. “But this approach, by its very nature, guarantees periodic failures — and the scale of those failures is growing as systems get more capable.”

Pointing to the recent breach of Hugging Face systems by OpenAI agents, as well as continuing revelations of OpenAI discovering more rogue agents , Robinson argued, “An environment where things like this can happen is no place to grow artificial minds that could be smarter than we are and that might not do what we want them to.”

Given the increased risk, Robinson argued that frontier AI companies need to start operating “like nuclear-power plants or busy airports, with layers of redundancy and careful, time-consuming planning, so that the occasional and inevitable human error does not open a door to disaster.”

But Robinson said that in his time at OpenAI, he “never encountered a colleague who had experience making airplanes fly safely or nuclear reactors run without melting down, or helping the financial system grow without collapsing.”
In response to Robinson’s essay, OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company continues to improve its safety measures.

“We’re making sure our models don’t become more capable than we can safely manage and secure, and we pause training or hold back models when we need to slow down,” Pusateri said in a statement. “We’re making significant changes to strengthen security in our research and testing environments, train models to not just complete tasks but do so responsibly, expand our work with third-party evaluators, and improve real-time monitoring so we can detect and respond to concerning behavior earlier in the training process .”

Beyond calling for changes in OpenAI’s culture, Robinson also said it’s time to ask bigger questions about alignment — something that he admitted could sound “touchy-feely,” but he said it’s critical as companies’ current “measures of how well” AI systems “match human values are coarse.”
“The smarter the industry lets models grow while these problems remain unsolved, the more dangerous our situation becomes,” he said.

Robinson’s departure was first reported by Business Insider . In his essay, he also acknowledged that he’s following an apparently a common step in the AI whistleblower playbook: He’s hired a PR firm . But he insisted, “The decision to speak out is mine alone.”

“Perhaps I should have stayed and fought for fundamental shifts in our staffing and culture, but in practice, my colleagues and I were so busy sprinting that we seldom had the chance to consider big changes, much less to actually make them,” Robinson said. “That’s why I concluded that stronger incentives for safety — coming from outside the company — are a big part of getting this right.”

extraction.body: Another safety researcher has walked away from OpenAI, with David Robinson becoming the latest employee to resign while raising alarms about the company's internal culture. Robinson's departure adds to growing concerns about how the ChatGPT maker handles AI safety as it races toward artificial general intelligence, marking yet another high-profile exit from the company's safety team. David Robinson didn't mince words when he walked away from OpenAI. The safety researcher's resignation letter, obtained by TechCrunch, paints a picture of a company whose internal culture has fundamentally shifted as it chases the artificial general intelligence prize. Robinson acknowledges he's become "something of a cliché" - another AI safety employee issuing dire warnings while heading for the exit. But that self-awareness doesn't diminish the weight of his concerns about how OpenAI operates behind closed doors. Robinson's departure follows a string of high-profile exits from OpenAI's safety teams, including co-founder Ilya Sutskever and safety researcher Jan Leike earlier this year. Both left citing concerns that the company was prioritizing flashy product releases over the careful safety work needed for increasingly powerful AI systems. OpenAI has been sprinting toward what CEO Sam Altman calls "superintelligence" - AI systems that could surpass human capabilities across virtually all domains. That race has intensified pressure inside the company, with multiple former employees describing a culture that's shifted from cautious research to aggressive commercialization. Safety researchers join OpenAI drawn by the mission of developing beneficial AI, then leave frustrated by what they see as corner-cutting and cultural problems that make their work impossible. Robinson's resignation adds another data point to this troubling trend. What makes Robinson's departure particularly significant is his willingness to go public with specific cultural criticisms. Previous exits have been more diplomatically handled, with departing researchers offering vague concerns about "alignment" between personal values and company direction. Robinson appears to be taking a more direct approach. The safety team brain drain comes as OpenAI faces mounting external pressure over its development practices. Competitors like Anthropic have positioned themselves as the more safety-conscious alternative, while regulators worldwide are scrambling to understand and oversee AI development. Industry observers note that losing safety talent isn't just a PR problem for OpenAI - it's a technical one. These researchers possess deep knowledge of the company's systems and the specific risks they pose. OpenAI transformed from a research lab into a commercial powerhouse worth over $80 billion, but that metamorphosis has apparently cost the company some of its founding principles. For Robinson, the cultural shift became impossible to ignore. His decision to speak publicly about a "broken" culture suggests the problems run deeper than typical workplace friction - pointing instead to fundamental disagreements about how AI development should proceed. The question now is whether OpenAI will address the underlying issues driving these departures or continue losing the safety expertise it claims to value. With each resignation, the company's credibility on AI safety takes another hit, potentially undermining its position as regulators and competitors circle. Robinson's resignation crystallizes a growing crisis of confidence in OpenAI's commitment to safe AI development. As the company races toward superintelligence, losing the very researchers tasked with ensuring that journey doesn't end in catastrophe sends a troubling signal to investors, regulators, and the public. The real test will be whether OpenAI can rebuild trust with its safety teams before more critical expertise walks out the door.

extraction.body: Rather than downloading another app, a growing number of agents can simply be texted like an ordinary person. You text it what you need, and it can remember context, connect to the apps and services you already use, and complete tasks on your behalf. That can mean scheduling an appointment, organizing a calendar, researching a trip, sending an email, making a reservation, shopping online, or reminding you about something days later. While Instinct is one of the buzziest AI agents at present, thanks to its $10 billion valuation after its latest funding round of $1 billion, there are many others also making a play for this space. Below are some of the most notable options so far, from general-purpose personal assistants to agents designed for families, travel, and work. Caddy is an AI assistant that turns the information scattered across your phone into things you can actually act on. It lives in iMessage for iPhone users and RCS for Android users, so there’s no separate app or inbox to constantly check. For instance, an email contains an appointment that needs to be added to your calendar or a friend sends a list of things to pick up. Instead of worrying about all the details getting buried, Caddy connects to your calendars and conversations, then identifies things that may require action. It can add events to your calendar, set reminders, keep track of follow-ups, and even do research for you. Caddy has been available in public beta since April 2026. Fambot is an AI-powered “chief of staff” for families, designed to bring together the many moving parts of family life, including school communications, sports activities, meal planning, calendars, and other day-to-day responsibilities, and turn them into an organized plan. The service is designed to work across both an app and text messages. Fambot is available on iOS devices, Android devices, and the web, and families can also interact with it directly over SMS. Every night, Fambot automatically sends a summary of the following day, including upcoming events, to-dos, and details such as school uniform or packing requirements. Parents can reply to those messages to ask questions, check information, or make changes to their calendar. Fambot currently connects to Gmail and Google Calendar, with support for Outlook and Apple Calendar planned for the future. The company launched in beta in early September 2026 and has raised $3.5 million in pre-seed funding. The service is currently free during the beta period, but Fambot expects to eventually charge roughly the equivalent of a Netflix subscription. Folk is designed to be an AI assistant you can reach through iMessage, WhatsApp, and Telegram. It can remember personal context, manage reminders, research topics, track flights, handle email, and perform real-world tasks such as restaurant reservations. Instinct first made headlines after raising $350 million at a $2.5 billion valuation. In September 2026, it raised $1 billion , valuing it at $10 billion. The always-available agent can take actions on your behalf, rather than simply answer questions. Users can communicate with Instinct by text or voice and connect it to the apps and services they already use, such as email, calendar, Google Workspace, and more. The company says early users have used Instinct for tasks ranging from planning trips and buying groceries to booking tickets and cancelling subscriptions. In September, Instinct began giving users dedicated email addresses for their assistants. The idea is to let Instinct create and manage accounts on a user’s behalf without filling the user’s personal inbox. The agent can use its address to sign up for services, contact businesses, follow up on requests, and handle tasks that require an email account. (However, this level of autonomy has also raised concerns about privacy and security .) It’s also begun rolling out support for placing calls . Martin is a general-purpose personal assistant reachable through SMS as well as phone, WhatsApp, email, Slack, and its own iOS app. It can help manage calendars, email, reminders, tasks, notes, and communications. It can also act on behalf of users by sending messages or making phone calls, while providing daily summaries of what needs attention. It’s a bit on the pricier side, with subscriptions starting at $21 per month. Ohai is another family assistant focused on helping households manage the constant stream of information and tasks involved in everyday family life. Users can send messages, forward emails, or make voice requests, and the assistant can transform them into schedules, reminders, and plans. It can also coordinate calendars, household chores, and meals across multiple members of a family. It includes a free basic option, but also offers different subscriptions based on family size, starting at $9.99 per month. Similar to the other family-focused agents, the idea behind Ollie is that families already have the information they need, but it lives across school messages, calendars, task lists, and group chats. Ollie aims to bring those pieces together and keep them in sync. It can keep track of calendars, emails, reminders, tasks, and other household details, then deliver relevant information to users through text. Its biggest differentiator from other agents is that Ollie is one of the first mainstream, family-focused AI assistants to achieve SOC 2 compliance, a widely used security standard. Launched in June 2026, Ollie offers a free tier, as well as paid plans starting at $25 per month for 150 messages. A $100-per-month plan includes up to 1,000 messages. Orbits also has an AI assistant that is focused on the household. It works through both the Orbits app and text messaging, and can bring together calendars, lists, and conversations while also carrying out tasks for you. That can include searching the web, making purchases, booking restaurants, changing appointments, and requesting quotes for household services. Additionally, Orbits can remind family members about chores, communicate with service providers, and help coordinate responsibilities beyond the immediate household. There’s a free plan available, which offers features like 15 minutes of calls per month, or there are paid plans, including $25 per month for 30 minutes of calls and $100 per month for 60 minutes. Poke launched in March 2026 as a general-purpose assistant that you can reach through text messaging. It can handle tasks involving calendars, planning, health and fitness, smart-home controls, photos, and other everyday activities. Poke became particularly notable in June 2026 when Apple approved Poke as the first AI agent on the Apple Messages for Business platform. A month later, parent company The Interaction Company of California was acquired by AI coding startup Cognition in a deal valued in the low nine figures. Rene is an AI personal assistant designed to be a user’s “best contact” rather than another productivity agent. It’s text-based and can turn natural-language conversations into tasks, reminders, summaries, and other follow-up actions. Rene also maintains context across conversations, allowing it to remember details and surface things that may need attention later. Additionally, it has a browser, can write code, shop for you, as well as create slides and images. The biggest differentiator with Tomo ’s personal assistant for iMessage is that, instead of being a private assistant that only you interact with, Tomo can become part of group conversations. Also, like other agents, it’s designed to help with goals, accountability, scheduling, and everyday organization. It also has the ability to send reminders, search the web, work with calendars and email, watch videos, and edit photos. Notably, when Fo encounters something it cannot handle on its own, Wajo says it can bring in a human assistant to finish the task. Fo launched publicly in September 2025 with a free tier, while heavier workloads and custom agents are available through a paid Pro offering.

extraction.body: The AI revolution is moving beyond chatbots and into your text messages. A growing ecosystem of AI agents now lives directly in SMS and messaging platforms, offering everything from general assistance to specialized help for families, travel planning, and workplace productivity. This shift represents a major evolution in how we interact with artificial intelligence - making it as simple as sending a text. The latest frontier in AI isn't happening in fancy apps or desktop software - it's taking place in the most basic communication tool we all use: text messages. A new generation of AI agents is embedding directly into SMS and popular messaging platforms, transforming how millions of people access artificial intelligence. Unlike traditional AI assistants that require dedicated apps or specific devices, these text-based agents work with any phone capable of sending messages. Users simply text a number or add a contact, then start conversing with AI systems designed for specific tasks and contexts. Text-based AI agents eliminate these barriers by meeting users where they already spend significant time. Family-focused agents lead this emerging category, helping parents coordinate schedules, track activities, and manage household tasks through group chats. Travel agents powered by AI can handle booking research, itinerary planning, and real-time trip updates via simple text exchanges. Workplace productivity agents integrate with team messaging to automate routine tasks and provide quick information lookups. The technology leverages advances in large language models while working within the constraints of text messaging. These agents must communicate clearly in short bursts, handle context switching between different conversation threads, and maintain personality consistency across extended interactions. Several startups are betting big on this messaging-first approach to AI deployment. It also opens AI access to demographics that might otherwise avoid more complex AI tools. The integration possibilities extend beyond simple SMS to include WhatsApp, Telegram, and other popular messaging services where users already manage personal and professional communications. The shift reflects broader changes in how people expect to interact with technology. Rather than downloading specific apps for every function, users increasingly prefer services that integrate into existing workflows and communication patterns. Security and privacy considerations remain paramount as these services handle sensitive personal and professional information through messaging channels. The messaging-based AI trend also highlights the ongoing evolution of conversational interfaces. While voice assistants like Amazon's Alexa dominated earlier AI adoption waves, text-based interactions offer advantages in privacy, context retention, and multi-tasking scenarios. The emergence of AI agents in text messaging represents a significant shift toward more accessible and integrated artificial intelligence. By removing the friction of separate apps and complex interfaces, these services could accelerate mainstream AI adoption while fundamentally changing how we think about digital assistance. As the technology matures, expect messaging-based AI to become as common as sending a regular text - and potentially much more powerful.

sources.title: AI Agents Invade Your Text Messages as Conversational AI Goes Mobile
passages: The AI revolution is moving beyond chatbots and into your text messages.
Unlike traditional AI assistants that require dedicated apps or specific devices, these text-based agents work with any phone capable of sending messages.
Text-based AI agents eliminate these barriers by meeting users where they already spend significant time.
The emergence of AI agents in text messaging represents a significant shift toward more accessible and integrated artificial intelligence.
The latest frontier in AI isn't happening in fancy apps or desktop software - it's taking place in the most basic communication tool we all use: text messages.
Travel agents powered by AI can handle booking research, itinerary planning, and real-time trip updates via simple text exchanges.

extraction.body: The AI revolution is moving beyond chatbots and into your text messages. A growing ecosystem of AI agents now lives directly in SMS and messaging platforms, offering everything from general assistance to specialized help for families, travel planning, and workplace productivity. This shift represents a major evolution in how we interact with artificial intelligence - making it as simple as sending a text. The latest frontier in AI isn't happening in fancy apps or desktop software - it's taking place in the most basic communication tool we all use: text messages. A new generation of AI agents is embedding directly into SMS and popular messaging platforms, transforming how millions of people access artificial intelligence. Unlike traditional AI assistants that require dedicated apps or specific devices, these text-based agents work with any phone capable of sending messages. Users simply text a number or add a contact, then start conversing with AI systems designed for specific tasks and contexts. Text-based AI agents eliminate these barriers by meeting users where they already spend significant time. Family-focused agents lead this emerging category, helping parents coordinate schedules, track activities, and manage household tasks through group chats. Travel agents powered by AI can handle booking research, itinerary planning, and real-time trip updates via simple text exchanges. Workplace productivity agents integrate with team messaging to automate routine tasks and provide quick information lookups. The technology leverages advances in large language models while working within the constraints of text messaging. These agents must communicate clearly in short bursts, handle context switching between different conversation threads, and maintain personality consistency across extended interactions. Several startups are betting big on this messaging-first approach to AI deployment. It also opens AI access to demographics that might otherwise avoid more complex AI tools. The integration possibilities extend beyond simple SMS to include WhatsApp, Telegram, and other popular messaging services where users already manage personal and professional communications. The shift reflects broader changes in how people expect to interact with technology. Rather than downloading specific apps for every function, users increasingly prefer services that integrate into existing workflows and communication patterns. Security and privacy considerations remain paramount as these services handle sensitive personal and professional information through messaging channels. The messaging-based AI trend also highlights the ongoing evolution of conversational interfaces. While voice assistants like Amazon's Alexa dominated earlier AI adoption waves, text-based interactions offer advantages in privacy, context retention, and multi-tasking scenarios. The emergence of AI agents in text messaging represents a significant shift toward more accessible and integrated artificial intelligence. By removing the friction of separate apps and complex interfaces, these services could accelerate mainstream AI adoption while fundamentally changing how we think about digital assistance. As the technology matures, expect messaging-based AI to become as common as sending a regular text - and potentially much more powerful.

extraction.body: Prime Day 2025 ends tonight, and Lifehacker is sharing the best sales based on product reviews, comparisons, and price-tracking tools before it's over. Sales are accurate at the time of publication, but prices and inventory are always subject to change.For the past few years, I've been putting up and taking down security cameras at a rate that has led neighbors to worry I'm a conspiracy theorist. But as I've tested cameras from every company you can think of, from Ring to Vosker, I've learned some things along the way. One singular company and product line allows me to do this: the Eufy Solocam line. Eufy SoloCam S340 Save $80 on the eufy SoloCam S340, now just $119.99. Use code WS7DV27MPDIJ at Eufy Get Deal Get Deal Save $80 on the eufy SoloCam S340, now just $119.99. Use code WS7DV27MPDIJ at Eufy eufy Security eufy SoloCam E30, Solar Powered, 360° Pan, AI Tracking, 2K Clarity, Security Cameras Wireless Outdoor, Camera, Outdoor Camera, HomeBase S380 Compatible, No Monthly Fee $99.98 at Amazon $149.99 Save $50.01 Get Deal Get Deal $99.98 at Amazon $149.99 Save $50.01 Eufy SoloCam S340 $139.99 at Amazon $199.99 Save $60.00 Get Deal Get Deal $139.99 at Amazon $199.99 Save $60.00 SEE 0 MORE I now have a Eufy doorbell, and Eufy cameras dot the inside and outside of my home. I use them for traditional purposes, like the E340 with floodlights that watches over my driveway, and non traditional (I have an E30 in my chicken coop). The solar power means you can install the cameras almost anywhere, with no need to run a cord or wiring. Eufy cameras are easy to set up—they're ready to go out of the box. Even the wired models, like the E340, come with easy instructions and a hook to help you wire them up. I am cautious around electrical work, but this was easy to do myself. All your cameras appear in a lineup, and it shows you a recent capture. Clicking on the picture takes you to a live view, and I'm always impressed at the speed with which the live view comes up, and that it almost never times out. These are both common problems on other apps. Words aren't mumbled, and you can hear voices crisply and clearly, without much lag, if you're using any of the cameras to have a conversation. You can easily tap an icon to take you to the number of clips captured by your cameras, and there are easy-to-use filters to help you quickly get to exactly the clip you want. I click into my Eufy app an unhealthy amount of times each day to see who's at the door, if the rat in my chicken coop is back, or to double check whether the trash service emptied my cans. It's basically a hard drive that lives near your internet router and networks all your cameras. For an additional $149.99, I think it's worth it.Eufy cameras are always a good value, but many of the models above are currently discounted as much as 35% off, making it an excellent time to stock up. Best Buy’s Prime Day competition sale, “Black Friday in July,” runs through Sunday, July 13 and has some of the best tech sales online. It’s an especially good option if you’re a My Best Buy “Plus” or “Total” member.Home Depot extended their 4th of July sale through at least July 9, competing with some amazing deals of their own. (Oct. 3, 2026) – The NHRA and World Wide Technology Raceway announced a sixth consecutive Saturday reserved seat sellout for the 15 th annual NAPA Auto Parts NHRA Midwest Nationals. “Today’s sold-out crowd at the NAPA Auto Parts NHRA Midwest Nationals is another tremendous showcase of the passion and enthusiasm St. Louis fans have for NHRA drag racing,” said NHRA President Glen Cromwell. “The team at World Wide Technology Raceway continues to provide an outstanding experience and it’s exciting to see another packed house in St. Louis during our 75th anniversary season.” Friday’s opening day featured fan activities and qualifying under the lights, setting the stage for another sold-out Saturday at World Wide Technology Raceway. passages: Boeing’s 737 Max 10 certification gets a boost after a Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) panel determined that a software glitch affecting certain 737 Max flight computers does not pose a safety risk.The FAA’s Corrective Action Review Board made the determination on Friday after examining the issue, which could occur when pilots abort a landing attempt.Following the report, Boeing shares rose 1.6% to $195.40 as of 2:47 p.m.
The smaller 737 Max 7 was certified in August with the affected software.
“The agency will also issue a special airworthiness information bulletin to US carriers and foreign regulators to ensure they’re aware of Boeing’s bulletin," the official said.
United has also said it is not accepting deliveries of new aircraft equipped with the glitch, while Southwest said recent and upcoming Max 8 deliveries would not have the malfunctioning software.

Boeing will issue a bulletin to airlines explaining how crews should respond if the malfunction occurs. “The agency will also issue a special airworthiness information bulletin to US carriers and foreign regulators to ensure they’re aware of Boeing’s bulletin," the official said. “We will continue to follow the lead of the FAA as our engineers work on the next software update,” Boeing said in a statement following the FAA’s determination. GE Aerospace, which supplies the software, said it supports the FAA’s decision and will continue working with Boeing on the update. The FAA’s decision removes a potential regulatory hurdle for Boeing’s 737 Max 10, the largest version of the Max family. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford had said earlier this week that certification of the aircraft would be delayed until the agency determined whether the software problem posed a safety risk. The Max 10 is already years behind schedule and is important to Boeing’s efforts to generate cash and strengthen its balance sheet. Are airlines flying aircraft with the glitch? Boeing customers Southwest Airlines, United Airlines, American Airlines and Alaska Air have separately said they do not operate aircraft with the affected software version. United has also said it is not accepting deliveries of new aircraft equipped with the glitch, while Southwest said recent and upcoming Max 8 deliveries would not have the malfunctioning software.

extraction.body: Boeing’s 737 Max 10 certification gets a boost after a Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) panel determined that a software glitch affecting certain 737 Max flight computers does not pose a safety risk.The FAA’s Corrective Action Review Board made the determination on Friday after examining the issue, which could occur when pilots abort a landing attempt.Following the report, Boeing shares rose 1.6% to $195.40 as of 2:47 p.m. New York time.Why did the FAA clear the software issue?The FAA said in its statement that the glitch is “not a safety concern” because pilots retain full control of the aircraft and the information displayed to the flight crew is clear and unambiguous.The issue can arise during a go-around, when a pilot decides to abandon a landing and climb again. Boeing will issue a bulletin to airlines explaining how crews should respond if the malfunction occurs. “The agency will also issue a special airworthiness information bulletin to US carriers and foreign regulators to ensure they’re aware of Boeing’s bulletin," the official said. “We will continue to follow the lead of the FAA as our engineers work on the next software update,” Boeing said in a statement following the FAA’s determination. GE Aerospace, which supplies the software, said it supports the FAA’s decision and will continue working with Boeing on the update. The FAA’s decision removes a potential regulatory hurdle for Boeing’s 737 Max 10, the largest version of the Max family. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford had said earlier this week that certification of the aircraft would be delayed until the agency determined whether the software problem posed a safety risk. The smaller 737 Max 7 was certified in August with the affected software. The Max 10 is already years behind schedule and is important to Boeing’s efforts to generate cash and strengthen its balance sheet. Are airlines flying aircraft with the glitch? Boeing customers Southwest Airlines, United Airlines, American Airlines and Alaska Air have separately said they do not operate aircraft with the affected software version. United has also said it is not accepting deliveries of new aircraft equipped with the glitch, while Southwest said recent and upcoming Max 8 deliveries would not have the malfunctioning software.

The funds’ combined net assets now stand at $109.3 billion, down 14.6% from the $128 billion peak reached in mid-January. The most significant selling took place early in the year. The funds experienced their worst day of 2026 in late January, when investors pulled a net $818 million shortly after the assets peaked in mid-January. This suggests investors sold most aggressively near the top.

A net figure subtracts total outflows from total inflows, meaning the funds can see billions move in either direction and still finish the year close to zero. This is why a strong quarter can mask a weak half.

August led the third quarter with net inflows of $3.5 billion, while September added another $2.7 billion, according to SoSoValue data. July had a modest inflow of roughly $170 million. The funds also recorded their best single day of the year in late September, with a net inflow of $999 million.

However, while quarterly totals reflect inflow movements, year-to-date figures indicate how much of that money remained. A report focusing solely on the $6.3 billion misses the significant $5.4 billion outflows that occurred earlier.

Despite this, the longer-term trend remains positive. Since their launch in January 2024, the funds have accumulated a net total of $57.6 billion, meaning the 2026 outflows have reduced that total without reversing it.

The flow totals show money exited the funds, but they don’t indicate who sold, and the issuers haven’t explained the outflows. Financial advisors and brokerage platforms hold a substantial portion of these spot ETFs , so such outflows typically suggest planned portfolio adjustments rather than panic selling.

Investors may have rebalanced their portfolios, reducing Bitcoin holdings to align with target allocations, or taken profits near the January peak. However, investors switching between different Bitcoin funds cannot account for the total outflows since such movements would net out in the overall figure.

Investors redeemed their shares, meaning they cashed out of the funds. This information may dampen the optimistic perception surrounding the third-quarter headline. The flow data also tests Citigroup ( NYSE:C | C Price Prediction ), which has linked its $113,000 Bitcoin price target to $5 billion in ETF inflows over 12 months.

Outflows contributed to this drop, and Bitcoin’s price also played a role, trading about 5% below its starting point for 2026 . So, where did the money from the first half go, and what might its return mean for the remainder of 2026? The year-to-date total of $985 million includes the $6.3 billion inflow in the third quarter, meaning the first half ended with around $5.4 billion in net outflows. This occurred even though the funds experienced a seven-week period of inflows in the spring, suggesting that selling outside that timeframe was more substantial. The most significant selling took place early in the year. The funds experienced their worst day of 2026 in late January, when investors pulled a net $818 million shortly after the assets peaked in mid-January. This suggests investors sold most aggressively near the top. Investors redeemed their shares, meaning they cashed out of the funds.
